policy_summary:
Overnight sleeping in vehicles, at the roadside or in car parks, is not permitted under NATIONAL PARK BYELAWS. That is a different legal basis from everything else recorded so far - not a parking order, not a PSPO, not a landowner's conditions of entry, but local law.

The Authority is careful to distinguish stopping from staying: pulling into a lay-by to admire the view and have a cup of tea is fine. Sleeping there is not. Motorhome users are directed to designated campsites.

It also publishes a Coach Driver and Motorhome Guide map, and warns that vehicle size puts some roads off limits and that satellite navigation should not be relied on.
notes:
IMPORTANT AND WIDELY MISUNDERSTOOD. Dartmoor is one of the very few places in England where wild camping is legally permitted - but for TENTS ONLY, pitched away from roads and attractions. That right does not extend to vehicles at all. People routinely assume Dartmoor's wild camping permission covers sleeping in a van. It does not, and the prohibition is a byelaw rather than a parking rule, so it applies at the roadside as well as in car parks.

First confirmed byelaw in the dataset. That takes the instrument count to six: off-street parking orders, on-street TROs, experimental TROs, PSPOs, opening hours, landowner policy - and now byelaws. The original scoping assumed one.

STEP-2 SWEEP, 27 July 2026 - the Authority's own land and property, camping barns, visitor centres and car parks were all checked and Dartmoor National Park Authority owns and runs NO campsite, caravan site, camping barn or aire, and permits no overnight vehicle stay anywhere. Its open-data land and property disclosure lists only car parks (thirty-odd, with Princetown, Meldon Reservoir, Postbridge and Haytor as the managed ones), Parke, and Higher Uppacott; there is no accommodation asset and no accommodation income line. Car parking income was GBP76,399 in 2019/20, described as managed car parks plus donations from cairns at the others, i.e. honesty boxes. The Authority also discloses that it 'does not fall under S.55 of the Road Traffic Regulation Act 1984' and so publishes no statutory parking account - a useful instrument-level fact, since it means DNPA car parks are not run under a council-style RTRA parking-order regime. The camping-and-motorhomes page states flatly: 'You cannot park your motorhome or campervan overnight in laybys, at the roadside, or in car parks.' No aire, pilot, trial or consultation was found for 2024-2026. The camping barns and bunkhouses the Authority points visitors to are third-party and farm-run; its own campsite directory lists commercial operators only.

Ownership corrections worth keeping, so nobody re-researches them as DNPA supply: Bellever is Forestry England and there is NO campsite there - 'Camping and overnight sleeping is not allowed in the forest' and 'Overnight stays are not allowed in the forest', car park included. Fernworthy sits on South West Water land and is managed by South West Lakes Trust, with no camping or motorhome provision (the Trust's camping is at Wimbleball). The sites in DNPA's directory - Barley Meadow, Glebe Park, Brimpts Farm, Dartmoor Caravan Park, Fox and Hounds, Langstone Manor, Lemonford, Lydford, River Dart and Tamar Valley - are all commercial and none involves a DNPA interest. Burrator, and the Duchy of Cornwall and National Trust holdings, were not reached.
open_questions: Which byelaws specifically, and from when? The Authority cites them without naming them.
How are they enforced, and what is the penalty? A byelaw breach is a criminal matter rather than a PCN.
Does the Authority run any car park where motorhomes may stay? Nothing found suggests so.
Is the same true of the Duchy of Cornwall and commons land within the park, which have separate ownership?
ANSWERED by the July 2026 sweep: the Authority runs no car park where motorhomes may stay, and owns no campsite, caravan site or camping barn at all.

Whether the byelaws are actually the instrument behind the CAR PARK prohibition is now doubtful. The byelaws are made under s.90 National Parks and Access to the Countryside Act 1949 and s.11 Dartmoor Commons Act 1985 and their operative text is about ACCESS LAND - no tent within 100m of a public road or in any enclosure, no camping in a tent on the same site for more than two consecutive nights, and no parking of 'a caravan or trailer unattached to a towing vehicle' on access land. A car park is not access land, and the caravan clause covers DETACHED caravans and trailers. The Authority asserts the car-park ban on its camping page but the cited byelaws may not support it; the real instrument may be separate car park byelaws or plain landowner conditions of entry. The confidence on the car park record should be read down accordingly.

The caravan byelaw contains an 'except on any area which is set apart and indicated by notice' carve-out. No evidence was found that any such area has ever been designated - which is itself the cleanest confirmation that the Authority provides nothing.

sites.name: Roadside and lay-bys throughout Dartmoor National Park
sites.notes: Overnight sleeping in a vehicle at the roadside is prohibited by byelaw. Stopping is fine - the Authority explicitly permits pulling into a lay-by for the view and a cup of tea. It is sleeping that is caught, and it is caught anywhere in the park, not only in car parks.

sites.name: All Dartmoor National Park car parks
sites.notes: Same byelaw prohibition. Users are directed to designated campsites that accept motorhomes.

sites.name: Wild camping rights (tents only)
sites.notes: Recorded because the confusion is so common. Dartmoor permits wild camping in TENTS, pitched away from roads and attractions, with no large groups. That right does not extend to vehicles. Having a legal right to wild camp on Dartmoor on foot does not mean you may sleep in a van there.
